title: The King who never answers to anyone, yet answers you
subtitle: Al-Malik: the true King, whose rule is total, eternal and good
intro: Al-Malik (الْمَلِكُ) means The King: the One whose command runs through everything, who rules without helpers, partners or anyone above Him, and whose reign never ends. Every other ruler borrows power for a while. Knowing this name frees you from fearing them and teaches you where to take your requests.

root.sense: The root carries the idea of holding firmly and having control. From it come mulk (rule, dominion), milk (property) and malik (king). A king in Arabic is one whose word is obeyed across a whole realm, who commands, forbids and runs the affairs of his people. Al-Malik is the one whose word is obeyed across all of existence.

picture.label: What kingship looks like when it is His

row.title: The powerful run my world
sub: the boss, the state, the market

knowing: A king is not the same as an owner. An owner controls a thing; a king governs a realm and its people, commands and forbids, and carries the burden of running it all. Al-Malik is {idea}King in the fullest sense: His command reaches everything, nothing in His realm is outside His rule, and His rule needs no one's permission{/idea}. Human rulers answer to parliaments, laws, allies or lenders. Many hold a title with little real say. Allah answers to no one, consults no one out of need, and is never overruled.

His kingship is also free of every flaw that stains human power. Kings grow anxious about rivals, cling to their thrones, and often become harsher and more tight-fisted the more they hold. Al-Malik has no rival to fear and loses nothing by giving. His reign did not begin and will not end. When the heavens are rolled up, He will ask whose the kingdom is that day, and answer that it belongs to Allah, the One, the Overpowering (40:16).

Notice the order in the last chapter of the Quran: Lord of mankind, King of mankind, God of mankind (114:1-3). Many people nurture and care for others; fewer are kings; only One is God. The name Al-Malik sits in the middle, reminding you that the One who looks after you also rules over everything that could harm you.
seeing: The Quran pairs His kingship with His will again and again: to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, He creates what He wills. A King's rule shows in His decisions, and the Quran shows His in creation, in history and in the Hereafter.

You see it in the rise and fall of empires. Pharaoh boasted of the rivers flowing beneath him; Musa told his frightened people that the earth belongs to Allah and He gives it to whom He wills, and that the end belongs to the mindful. Then he warned them that being given power would itself be a test of how they behave. Every dictator who planned to rule forever met the one appointment no guard can stop.

And you see it in the most tender place. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ told that in the night Allah descends in a way that befits His majesty and says: I am the King, I am the King. Who is calling on Me, that I may answer? Who is asking, that I may give? Who is seeking forgiveness, that I may forgive? The King of all kings opens His court to anyone awake.
trusting: When a manager bullies you, a landlord threatens you, or the news fills you with dread about who holds power, remember that {idea}every authority over you is a borrowed one, granted by Al-Malik and taken back on His schedule{/idea}. You still act, speak up and seek justice. But you stop {trap}treating people with power as if they were the final word on your life{/trap}.

It also changes how you ask. We are bold with bosses and shy with Allah. In a hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, Allah says that if every human and jinn from first to last stood in one place and asked, and He gave each one everything they asked, it would decrease His kingdom no more than a needle dipped into the sea. So ask the King for big things: healing, guidance, a righteous family, the highest Paradise. {reward}A request is never too large for the One whose treasury cannot shrink{/reward}.
loving: Human kings keep their distance. Their power makes them cold, and their gates are guarded. Al-Malik is the reverse: the greatest King is the most generous, and He calls out to His subjects rather than waiting to be petitioned. {reward}The heart cannot help loving a King whose majesty never makes Him stingy and whose rule is never unjust.{/reward} To be His servant is not humiliation; it is the safest place in all of existence.
now: It is 3am and you are awake again, scrolling headlines about elections, prices and wars you cannot control. Put the phone down. {idea}At this exact hour the King of all kings is asking who will call on Him.{/idea} Make wudu, stand for two short units of prayer, and hand Him the worries that belong to His kingdom anyway.
old: I feel at the mercy of whoever is in charge: governments, employers, people with money and influence.
new: They are tenants on a short lease in a kingdom that belongs to Al-Malik, and He hears me directly.
try: Before sleeping tonight, set an alarm for the last part of the night, and if you wake, ask Allah for one thing you have been too shy to ask for.

dua.text: O Allah, You are the King; there is no god but You. You are my Lord and I am Your servant. I have wronged myself and I admit my sins, so forgive me all my sins, for none forgives sins but You.
dua.note: The Prophet ﷺ began his prayer with words like these, as reported in Sahih Muslim; they are a fitting way to stand before Al-Malik, especially in the quiet of the night.

pairs.why: Al-Malik is the King who rules and commands; Malik-ul-Mulk is the Owner of all dominion, who hands out and takes back every human kingdom.
In 59:23 and 62:1 Al-Malik is followed by Al-Quddus: His kingship is pure of the greed, fear and injustice that stain every human throne.

faq.a: Al-Malik means The King. It describes Allah as the One whose command reaches all of creation, who rules without partner or helper, who answers to no one, and whose reign has no beginning or end. Every human king rules only a part of the earth, for a time, and by His permission.

faq.q: What is the difference between Al-Malik and Malik-ul-Mulk?
faq.a: Al-Malik stresses kingship: authority, command and governing all affairs. Malik-ul-Mulk stresses ownership of dominion itself: Allah owns every kingdom and gives it to whom He wills and takes it from whom He wills (3:26). Together they say that He rules everything and owns everything.

faq.q: Is it Maliki or Maaliki yawm al-din in Al-Fatiha?
faq.a: Both are authentic recitations of 1:4. One reads Maliki (King of the Day of Judgment), the other Maaliki (Owner of the Day of Judgment). Scholars note that the two readings together affirm both meanings: on that Day, Allah alone is King and alone is Owner.

faq.q: Can a person be called Malik?
faq.a: Yes. The word malik is used in the Quran for human kings, such as the king of Egypt in the story of Yusuf. What belongs to Allah alone is absolute kingship. A human may hold a title, but only Allah is the King whose rule is complete, independent and everlasting.
